analysis.one_liner: Shields respirator makers from lawsuits over government-approved designs, even in cases already filed.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote in the Senate and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred nearly all lawsuits against respirator makers and sellers claiming a defective design or warning, as long as the device carried a federal NIOSH safety approval and was built to that approved design. It would have wiped out state laws on these claims, and it would have applied even to lawsuits already in court that had not yet reached trial. The only exception: a manufacturer could still be sued if it hid information from NIOSH or bribed a NIOSH official to win approval.
analysis.who_benefits: Respirator manufacturers and sellers, who would be largely shielded from product liability suits over NIOSH-approved designs, including suits already pending when the bill took effect.

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer or seller could not be sued for defective design or defective warnings if the respirator received NIOSH approval and was built in compliance with the NIOSH-approved design and labeling in effect on the manufacture date.
The bill would supersede any state or local laws covering such claims, so no state could offer stronger protections to injured workers.
It would apply to any pending civil action in federal or state court that had not yet proceeded to trial when enacted, regardless of when the respirator was made or sold.
The bill's stated rationale was that litigation costs might drive manufacturers out of the market, and that losing domestic respirator production would put workers and emergency responders at risk.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and emergency responders harmed by defective respirators would lose the ability to sue, including people whose lawsuits were already filed; state and local laws protecting them would be overridden.

drawbacks.text: A worker or responder sickened or injured by a respirator with an approved but allegedly defective design or warning would have no claim, even if the case was already in court and had not reached trial.
The federal preemption would override any state or local law offering stronger remedies for these claims.
A statute of limitations for the narrow fraud and bribery exceptions would not begin running until NIOSH formally withdrew approval, which could leave even those claims unresolved for years.

Supporters would argue the shield was needed to keep manufacturers making respirators, and the bill did preserve liability where a maker misled NIOSH or bribed an official, or failed to comply with the approved design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts nearly all the cost of defective government-approved respirators from manufacturers to injured workers, while keeping the courts open only for proven fraud or bribery of regulators. The theoretical public benefit — keeping manufacturers in the market — rests on the claim that litigation costs threaten respirator supply, a claim the bill asserts in its findings but does not demonstrate.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Cornyn introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cornyn introduced the Respirator Access Assurance Act of 2005 on July 14, 2005.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was ever recorded.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Respirator makers did not get the liability shield they sought, and injured workers kept their existing right to sue under state law. Nobody gained much: the bill simply disappeared in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured workers kept their right to sue

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, with introductory remarks, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no markup, no vote, and the bill was never reported out or scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were involved — a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor — and the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have immunized them from defective-design and defective-warning lawsuits over NIOSH-approved respirators, including suits already filed. The cost would have fallen on workers hurt by those devices.
The bill would have eliminated most claims these lawyers could bring for workers hurt by approved respirator designs, and would have killed pending cases that had not reached trial.
